rationale: B wins because it keeps the proof gates closer to the angles instead of letting the headline outrun the facts. Its data angle says, "Without the underlying numbers this angle is a press release," which is exactly the warning a founder needs before touching a non-peer-reviewed internal study; A, meanwhile, leads with "rivals still charge for it" and later reaches for "teachers already stretched thin," neither of which is in the supplied update. Both sets have real bones, but B is cleaner strategic material.
gaps_in_A: "rivals still charge for it" and "paid commercial products versus a large donor-funded free entrant" assert competitor pricing and market structure the update does not give.
"teachers already stretched thin" imports a teacher-burnout frame without any workload data in the facts. It may be true in the world; it is not proven here.
"which 30 districts are getting Khanmigo" is dismissed as a "duplicate," but the real problem is missing names. If district names exist, localizing the rollout is a legitimate angle, not a duplicate.
The next step, "fact-check," is too narrow. The set also needs named districts, teacher sources, donor details, and competitor pricing before the strongest angles can leave the building.
gaps_in_B: "one of the largest AI-tutoring deployments" is not in the update. One million additional students is large; "one of the largest" needs proof.
"while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat" and "typically a paid product" make the same unsupported competitor-pricing leap B otherwise warns about.
"landing in named districts" is not supplied. The classroom angle is useful, but it should be framed as conditional until Khan can name a district and teacher.
"journalist-fit-check" as the next step is a little premature. The set admits most angles are gated on methodology or named sources; get those assets first, then pick the reporter.
